title: Display Interface
story: Your debugger prints `[object]` for everything — useless! You want every type in your system to be printable. A Person shows their name, a Score shows the number, a Date shows the formatted string. Time to build a universal Display interface that makes ANY type printable.
why: The Display interface pattern is universal — every language has a 'convert to string' mechanism, and understanding it teaches you how to design interfaces that make heterogeneous systems work together.
analogy: The Display interface is like a name tag at a conference — every attendee (type) wears one, but the tag shows different information: 'Alex, Engineer' for a person, 'RX-9000, Robot' for a machine. The tag format (method signature) is the same; the content is unique to each type.
try_it: Add Displayable to three more types: `Movie` (title + year), `Coordinate` (x, y), and `Event` (name + date). Create a Vec of each type and use `print_all` to display them. Then ask: what if you want to display the same type in different formats (short vs long)? You'd need either parameters (which interfaces don't allow) or multiple interfaces (DisplayShort, DisplayLong).
tips: One interface = one responsibility — Display means 'human-readable text,' not 'machine format' or 'debug info'
The `.display()` method typically uses string concatenation and conversion functions like `string.int_to_str`
Every type with display can be passed to ANY generic function constrained by Displayable — maximum reuse
common_mistakes: Building display logic into the main function instead of the type — display should live with the type, not the caller
Making one mega-interface instead of focused ones — 'Printable + Serializable + Comparable' should be three separate interfaces
Returning incomplete info from display — include enough fields to identify the value, not just one field
